questions.stem: White light passes through a prism and splits into a spectrum. This happens because:

options.text: The prism adds colour to the light
Different colours of light have different speeds in glass, causing them to refract by different amounts
The prism reflects different colours at different angles
Only some colours can pass through glass

questions.explanation: White light is a mixture of all colours, each with a different wavelength. In glass, different wavelengths travel at slightly different speeds, causing each colour to refract (bend) by a different amount. Violet light slows down the most and bends the most; red light bends the least. This process is called dispersion. The prism does not add colour (option A) — it separates the colours already present.

questions.stem: A red filter is placed in front of a white light source. What colours of light pass through the filter?
questions.explanation: A colour filter works by absorbing all colours except its own colour. A red filter absorbs blue, green, yellow, violet, and all other colours, transmitting only red light. Option A describes the opposite of what happens. Option D is a common misconception — the filter does not 'tint' the light; it removes wavelengths entirely.

questions.stem: A blue object is illuminated with red light only. What colour does the object appear?
questions.explanation: A blue object appears blue in white light because it reflects blue wavelengths and absorbs other colours. When illuminated with only red light, there is no blue light to reflect. The object absorbs the red light and reflects nothing — so it appears black. Option A is wrong because there is no blue light available to reflect. Option B (purple) would require both red and blue light. Option C is wrong because the object absorbs red light.

questions.stem: The three primary colours of light are red, green, and blue. When red light and green light overlap on a white screen, what colour is produced?
questions.explanation: In additive colour mixing (mixing light), red + green = yellow. This is different from mixing paints (subtractive mixing), where red + green would give a muddy brown. White (option D) is produced when all three primary colours (red + green + blue) are combined. TV and phone screens use this principle — yellow pixels are created by combining red and green sub-pixels.

questions.stem: A white object is viewed through a cyan filter. What colour does the object appear?
questions.explanation: A white object reflects all colours of light. A cyan filter transmits cyan light (which is blue + green) and absorbs red. So only the cyan component passes through the filter, making the object appear cyan. Option A is wrong because the filter removes the red component. Option B is wrong because red is the colour that gets absorbed. Cyan is a secondary colour made from blue + green.
